title: Morning inbox sort into labeled queues
summary: Each morning SI sorts the shared inbox into clear queues. It flags what is urgent. It leaves draft replies for a person to review.
problem: A shared inbox mixes customer questions, vendor mail, invoices, newsletters, and spam. Urgent messages get buried. The first hour of the day goes to figuring out what needs attention. That time should go to answering it.
what_si_does: SI reads new messages. It applies labels you define. Examples: new request, existing customer, billing, vendor, needs owner, ignore. It pulls out the key detail for each. That can be a job address, an account name, or a requested date. It marks anything time-sensitive. It writes a short summary at the top of each queue. It leaves draft replies for routine questions. Nothing goes out without a person pressing send.
setup: Connect the inbox with permission to read, label, and draft, but not send. Write down your queue names. Write what counts as urgent. Add a handful of good past replies to match your tone. Setup is often a few days. Then you spend a week or two adjusting the rules.
human_checks: A person reviews and sends every draft. SI never sends on its own.
Messages SI is unsure about go to a 'needs a human' queue. SI does not guess.
Labels and urgency rules are reviewed after the first couple of weeks. Then they are adjusted.

examples.scenario: Overnight emails are split into emergency calls, such as no heat or an active leak. New estimate requests have the address and problem pulled out. Supplier mail is in its own pile. The dispatcher starts with the emergencies.

During busy season, client emails are labeled by client and topic. Topics include a missing document, a question about a return, and payment. Anything that mentions a notice or deadline is flagged for a partner.
Tenant emails are sorted into maintenance, rent, and lease questions. Prospective-tenant inquiries go in their own queue. Maintenance messages are marked by urgency.

copy_prompt: Go through the unread messages in [inbox] from the last [24 hours]. Label each one as [list of queues]. Mark anything that mentions [urgent terms, e.g. leak, deadline, cancel] as urgent. For each message, write a one-line summary and pull out [key details, e.g. address, account, date]. Draft replies only for messages that match these examples: [paste 3-5 good past replies]. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: The day starts with a sorted list instead of a raw inbox. Urgent messages are less likely to sit unseen.

title: A weekly list of emails still waiting on you
summary: Once a week SI finds threads still waiting on your reply. A customer, client, or vendor may be waiting. SI lists them with a suggested next step.
problem: Some emails get read and set aside for later. Then they never get answered. Nobody notices until the other person follows up. They are annoyed, or they take their business elsewhere.
what_si_does: SI scans received and sent mail for the past few weeks. It finds threads where the last message came from someone else. That message asked a question or requested something. It skips newsletters, notifications, and threads that were clearly closed. The result is a short list. It is grouped by who is waiting, how long they have waited, and what they asked. Simple ones get a draft reply.
setup: Read access to the mailbox. Add draft access if you want replies drafted. Give a list of senders or domains to ignore. Setup is often a day or two.
human_checks: A person decides which threads actually need a reply. That person sends any drafts.
Threads involving complaints or money are flagged for the owner. They are not drafted.
The ignore list is updated as false alarms show up.

examples.scenario: Friday afternoon, the principal gets a list of six client and consultant emails with open questions. One is a structural engineer waiting on a drawing revision for nine days.
The list shows two clients who asked about adding a driver to their policy. They never heard back. A carrier underwriter is waiting on a signed form.
Three inquiry emails about spring events are surfaced. Each includes the requested date and headcount. This happens before those dates get booked by someone else.

copy_prompt: Look through my inbox [mailbox] for the last [21] days. Find threads where the most recent message is from someone else and they asked a question or requested something. Ignore [newsletters, notifications, these senders]. List each one with who is waiting, how many days, and what they asked. Draft short replies for the simple ones only. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Fewer people fall through the cracks. The weekly list makes it easier to close loops. That happens before they turn into complaints.

title: Answering 'where is it?' questions from your own records
summary: A customer asks about an order, job, repair, or application. SI looks it up in your system. Then it drafts an accurate reply.
problem: Many incoming messages are some version of 'where is my thing?' Answering each one means opening another system. Then you find the record and write the same kind of message again.
what_si_does: SI spots status questions. It finds the matching record by name, number, address, or email. It reads the current state. That can be shipped with a tracking number. It can be a technician scheduled. It can be a part on order. It can be waiting on the customer. It drafts a reply in your tone with the real details. It flags cases where the record looks stuck. It also flags cases that contradict what the customer was told.
setup: Give read access to the system that holds status. That can be an order system, a job tool, a repair log, or a shared sheet. Also give access to the inbox or helpdesk. Share a few example replies. Write the rules for when a delay should go to a person. Setup is often several days.
human_checks: A person approves each reply until the drafts are right most of the time. They can keep approving after that.
Anything that looks stuck or overdue goes to a person. The record is attached.
SI does not promise dates that are not in the record.

examples.scenario: A customer emails asking about their dishwasher. SI finds the ticket. The part is on backorder with an expected date. SI drafts a reply with that date and an offer to call.
A homeowner asks when installation will happen. SI checks the production board. The doors are in finishing. SI drafts a reply with the current stage and the scheduled install week.
A 'where is my order' email is matched to the order. Tracking shows it stalled for five days. The draft apologizes and offers a replacement option. The owner still must approve it.

copy_prompt: For each message in [inbox/queue] asking about the status of [an order/job/repair], find the matching record in [system or file] using [order number, name, email or address]. Draft a reply that states the current status and next step using only what is in the record. Flag any record with no update in [5] days. Use this tone: [example reply]. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Routine status questions get faster, more accurate answers. Stuck jobs or orders come to light sooner.

title: Refunds, returns and cancellations checked against your policy
summary: SI checks each refund, return, cancellation, or reschedule request against your written policy. Then it drafts the answer for approval.
problem: Requests to cancel, return, or get money back are handled differently depending on who answers. Some get approved that should not. Others get refused that should have been honored. Both lead to friction.
what_si_does: SI reads the request. It finds the relevant record. That can be the purchase date, booking date, deposit paid, or contract terms. It compares that with your written policy. It labels the request as clearly within policy, clearly outside, or a judgment call. It drafts the reply with the reason in plain language. Judgment calls go to the owner with the facts laid out.
setup: Give SI your written policy. Give read access to the records. Point to the inbox or form where requests arrive. Setup is often a few days. Most of that time is spent turning an informal policy into clear rules.
human_checks: A person approves every refund, credit, or fee waiver. SI never issues money.
Judgment calls and upset customers go to the owner.
The policy document is the source of truth. SI does not invent exceptions.

examples.scenario: A member asks to cancel mid-contract after moving. SI checks the membership terms. It finds the relocation clause. It drafts a reply listing the proof needed.
A couple asks to move their date. SI checks the contract's change terms and deposit rules. It drafts options for the manager to choose between.
A return request arrives 40 days after delivery. SI notes it is outside the 30-day window. The item was delivered damaged. SI marks it as a judgment call.

copy_prompt: Here is my policy for [refunds/returns/cancellations]: [paste]. For each request in [inbox/form], find the record in [system/file], and decide whether it is within policy, outside policy, or a judgment call. Draft a reply that explains the decision in plain language. List judgment calls separately with the facts. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Requests get consistent answers. The owner only sees the cases that need a real decision.

title: Building an FAQ from answers you have already written
summary: SI reads past replies to customers. It groups the questions that keep coming up. Then it drafts a plain FAQ or help page for you to edit.
problem: The same questions arrive every week. The best answers are scattered across old emails. Different people wrote them. New staff reinvent answers. Customers cannot find them on their own.
what_si_does: SI goes through a few months of sent replies. It groups similar questions. It picks the clearest past answer for each. Then it rewrites it into a short FAQ entry. It notes where past answers disagreed so you can decide which is right. It lists questions that may deserve a policy rather than an answer.
setup: An export of a few months of replies, or read access to the helpdesk. Setup is often a few days. Then you spend editing time on your side.
human_checks: The owner approves every answer before it is published.
Conflicting past answers are resolved by a person.
Anything involving prices, guarantees, or legal terms is double-checked.

examples.scenario: Past emails produce entries on vaccine schedules, what to bring to a first visit, and after-hours emergency options. The front desk reviews them.
Questions about access hours, unit sizes, insurance, and move-out notice become a single page. Staff can link to it.
Repeated client questions about support hours, change requests, and billing become an onboarding FAQ. It is sent with every new contract.

copy_prompt: Read these past replies [export or folder]. Group the questions that come up more than [3] times. For each group, write a short FAQ entry using the clearest past answer, in plain language. List any groups where past answers disagree. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Fewer repeat questions. Faster onboarding of new staff. Answers that match from person to person.

title: Replies to online reviews and public comments
summary: SI watches reviews, comments, and messages on your public pages. It flags the ones worth answering. Then it drafts replies in your voice.
problem: Reviews and comments arrive on several platforms. Answering them slips. Negative reviews sit unanswered for weeks. Genuine questions in comments get lost among the noise.
what_si_does: SI collects new reviews and comments. It sorts them into praise, question, complaint, and spam. It drafts short replies for the ones that need one. Complaints get a careful, non-defensive draft. That draft offers to take the talk offline. Complaints are flagged for the owner. SI never argues. SI never reveals private details.
setup: Access or exports from the review and social platforms you use. Plus a few examples of replies you like. Setup is often a few days.
human_checks: Every public reply is approved by a person before posting.
Complaints go straight to the owner. So does anything mentioning safety, injury, or legal threats.
Replies never include private customer details.

examples.scenario: A two-star review about a long wait gets a calm draft. It acknowledges the night, without excuses. It invites the guest to contact the manager.
Questions in social comments about insurance claims are flagged. The draft points people to call for an estimate.
Positive reviews get short thank-you drafts. Those drafts avoid confirming the reviewer is a patient.

copy_prompt: Here are new reviews and comments from [platforms] since [date]: [paste or export]. Sort them into praise, question, complaint and spam. Draft a reply for each praise, question and complaint in this tone: [examples]. Keep complaints calm, short and offer to continue privately. Do not mention any personal details. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Reviews and comments get answered more often in the same way. The owner sees complaints early.
caution: Medical, dental, and other health practices should never confirm someone is a patient. Do not discuss care in a public reply. Keep replies generic. Check privacy rules that apply to you.

title: A website or messaging chat assistant that hands hard cases to a person
summary: SI answers common questions in chat from your own website and documents. It passes anything unusual to a person. The chat is attached.
problem: People ask the same questions in chat or messaging apps at all hours. Either someone answers late. Or the chat widget is a form that just says we will get back to you.
what_si_does: SI answers from an approved set of sources. Those sources are your website, FAQ, price list, and policies. It can collect details for a quote or booking request. When a question falls outside its sources, it stops. It also stops if the question involves a complaint. It also stops if the person asks for a human. It says someone will follow up. Then it sends the chat summary to staff.
setup: An approved knowledge source. The chat or messaging tool. Clear rules for handoff. Setup is often one to two weeks. That includes testing with real questions.
human_checks: SI answers only from approved sources. It says so when it does not know.
Anything involving money, complaints, or exceptions is handed to a person.
Staff review a sample of chats each week. They correct answers.

examples.scenario: A visitor asks whether spring cleanups are still available in their town. SI confirms the service area. It collects the address and yard size. Then it sends the request to the office.
SI answers questions about office hours, consultation fees, and what documents to bring. It hands any question about a specific case to staff.
SI explains class levels and start dates. It collects placement-test requests.

copy_prompt: Using only these sources [website pages, FAQ, price list], answer customer questions in [chat/WhatsApp]. If a question is not covered, involves a complaint or money, or the person asks for a human, say that someone will follow up within [time] and send a summary to [staff contact]. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Common questions get answered when the office is closed. Staff pick up the chats that need them. They have the context in hand.
caution: Law, medical, and financial offices: the assistant should share general office facts only. It should never share anything that reads as advice on a specific situation.

title: After-hours and busy-time phone coverage
summary: A voice assistant answers calls you would miss. It handles common questions. It takes detailed messages or requests. Then it sends staff a summary.
problem: Calls that go to voicemail often never call back. Small offices cannot staff the phone through lunch, evenings, and weekends. Busy moments mean the person on the phone cannot also serve the person in front of them.
what_si_does: When nobody picks up, a voice assistant answers with your greeting. It handles a short list of approved questions. Those include hours, location, services, and how to book. It takes a structured message: name, number, reason, urgency. For true emergencies it follows your escalation rule. That can mean forwarding to the on-call phone. Staff get a text or email summary of each call.
setup: A phone number or forwarding rule. The approved question list. Your escalation rules. A message format. Setup is often one to two weeks. That includes test calls.
human_checks: Callers are told they are speaking with an automated assistant.
Emergency rules are tested before going live. They are reviewed regularly.
Staff return every message. The assistant does not make commitments on price or timing beyond what you approved.

examples.scenario: A 9 p.m. no-heat call is identified as urgent. It is forwarded to the on-call technician. A request for a maintenance quote becomes a message for the morning.
Over lunch the assistant gives office hours and directions. It takes callback messages. Anything that sounds urgent goes to the instructions you approved.
After hours, callers' location and vehicle details are collected. They are texted to the driver on duty.

copy_prompt: Draft a phone script for after-hours calls to [business]. It should greet callers, say it is an automated assistant, answer only these questions [list], take a message with name, number, reason and urgency, and treat these situations as emergencies [list] by [forwarding to number]. Write the summary text staff will receive. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Fewer missed calls turn into lost customers. Staff start the day with clear messages instead of voicemails.
caution: Call recording and automated calls are regulated. Consent rules differ by state and country. Disclose the assistant and any recording. Check the rules that apply before going live. Medical practices should keep the assistant away from clinical questions.

title: Follow-ups for quotes and estimates that went quiet
summary: SI finds quotes and estimates with no reply after a set number of days. Then it drafts a short, specific follow-up for each one.
problem: Quotes go out and then nothing happens. Following up feels awkward and gets skipped. Work is lost to whoever simply called back.
what_si_does: SI checks your quotes or estimates for ones still open after a set period. It reads what was quoted and any notes. It drafts a short follow-up that refers to the actual job. It suggests a different angle on the second follow-up. That can be a question or a scheduling option. It marks quotes to close out after the last attempt.
setup: Read access to where quotes live. That can be an estimating tool, CRM, accounting system, or a folder of PDFs. Draft access to email. Your follow-up timing. Setup is often a few days.
human_checks: A person approves each follow-up before it is sent.
Quotes the owner wants to handle personally are excluded.
Nothing is discounted or changed without the owner's decision.

examples.scenario: Twelve estimates from the last month are open. Each gets a draft that mentions the roof type. It also mentions the crew's next opening in that neighborhood.
A quote for event banners has had no reply for a week. The draft asks whether the event date is still on. It notes the latest order date for delivery in time.
Prospects who received a monthly-service proposal get a follow-up. It offers a short call to walk through the scope.

copy_prompt: Here are open quotes [file/export] with date sent, customer, job and amount. For each quote older than [7] days with no reply, draft a short follow-up that mentions the specific job and offers [a next step]. For quotes already followed up [2] times, suggest closing them. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: More quotes get a timely follow-up. The pipeline reflects what is really still open.

title: Turning form and email inquiries into clean CRM records
summary: SI reads each new inquiry from forms and email. It creates or updates the CRM contact. It logs what they want and the next step.
problem: Leads arrive through web forms, email, phone messages, and referrals. Some get entered twice. Some never get entered. The notes are too thin to follow up well.
what_si_does: SI reads each inquiry. It checks for an existing contact to avoid duplicates. It fills in the record. That includes name, company, and contact details. It includes what they asked for. It includes budget or timing if mentioned. It includes how they found you. It assigns the lead by your rules. It drafts the first reply or creates the follow-up task.
setup: Write access to the CRM limited to contacts, deals, and tasks. Plus the form tool and inbox. Your assignment rules. Setup is often a few days.
human_checks: Someone reviews new records daily at first. Then they spot-check.
First replies are approved before sending.
Merging suspected duplicates is confirmed by a person.

examples.scenario: A contact-form inquiry with date, venue, and guest count becomes a lead. The date is checked against the calendar. A draft reply lists packages.
An email asking for nightly cleaning of a 6,000 square foot office is logged. Size, frequency, and location are included. It is assigned to the estimator for a walkthrough.
Web inquiries are logged with the type of matter and referral source. A conflict-check task is created before anyone replies.

copy_prompt: For each new inquiry in [form/inbox], check [CRM] for an existing contact by email and phone. Create or update the contact with name, company, what they need, timing, budget if stated and source. Assign using [rules]. Draft a first reply using [template]. List any possible duplicates for me to confirm. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Leads are logged the same way each time. The first response goes out sooner. Notes are better for whoever follows up.

title: Call notes into a follow-up email and tasks
summary: After a sales or client call, SI turns your notes or the transcript into a recap email. It also makes CRM updates and dated tasks.
problem: After a call, the follow-up email and the CRM update are the first things to slip. Details are forgotten. Promised next steps happen late or not at all.
what_si_does: SI starts from typed notes, a voice memo, or a call transcript. It writes a short recap. The recap covers what the client needs and what was agreed. It covers open questions. It covers who does what by when. It drafts the follow-up email. It updates the CRM fields. It creates tasks with due dates.
setup: A way to get notes or transcripts to SI. Access to the CRM and email drafts. Setup is often a day or two.
human_checks: The person who was on the call reviews the recap and email before sending.
Pricing or commitments in the recap are checked against what was actually said.
Recording only happens with the consent required where you operate.

examples.scenario: A discovery call transcript becomes a recap. It lists the client's goals and the two campaigns discussed. It includes a promise to send a proposal by Thursday. A task is created for it.
A rep's voice memo from a site visit becomes notes. The notes cover roof orientation and the homeowner's financing question. A follow-up email has the requested information.
Notes from a call with a medical office about backups become a task list. An email confirms the next meeting.

copy_prompt: Here are my notes or transcript from a call with [client]: [paste]. Write a recap with needs, decisions, open questions and next steps with owners and dates. Draft a follow-up email in my voice. List the CRM fields to update and tasks to create. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Follow-ups go out while the call is fresh. The CRM reflects what was actually agreed.
caution: Call recording: consent rules differ by state and country. Some require every party to agree. Tell participants. Follow the stricter rule if you are unsure.

title: First-draft proposals from discovery notes
summary: SI turns discovery notes and your past proposals into a structured first draft. The draft has scope, timeline, and pricing options for you to edit.
problem: Proposals take hours to write. They often start from a copy of an old one. Leftover details from another client remain. The delay means the prospect waits while interest cools.
what_si_does: SI reads the discovery notes and a few of your past proposals. Then it drafts a proposal in your usual structure. It states the client's situation in their words. It covers scope and what is not included. It covers timeline. It covers pricing options from your rate sheet. It covers next steps. It highlights any section where it lacked information. It does not guess.
setup: Your proposal template. A rate sheet. Two or three good past proposals. Setup is often a day or two.
human_checks: The owner reviews scope and pricing line by line.
SI does not invent pricing. It uses the rate sheet and flags gaps.
Nothing is sent to the prospect without approval.

examples.scenario: Notes from a walkthrough become a proposal. It covers demolition, plumbing, and tile scope. It includes an allowance line for fixtures. It flags that cabinet sizes are still unknown.
A discovery call becomes a proposal with three package options. The timeline is built from the studio's standard phases.
Notes from a meeting with a 40-person company become a proposal outline. It includes the review steps. One section is marked for the consultant to fill in.

copy_prompt: Using these discovery notes [paste], my template [file], rate sheet [file] and these past proposals [files], draft a proposal for [client]. Include situation, scope, exclusions, timeline, [2-3] pricing options and next steps. Mark any section where information is missing. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Proposals go out sooner. They start from a clean, client-specific draft instead of a recycled one.

title: A one-page brief on a prospect before you meet
summary: Before a meeting or pitch, SI gathers public facts about the prospect. It also gathers your past contact. Then it writes a short brief.
problem: Walking into a meeting unprepared costs credibility. Researching every prospect takes time nobody has. Past emails and notes about the account are scattered.
what_si_does: SI reads the prospect's website, recent public news, and any public profiles you point it to. It also reads your own CRM notes and past emails. It produces a one-page brief. The brief covers what they do. It covers size and locations if public. It covers recent changes. It covers who you are meeting. It covers past contact. It lists three questions worth asking. Sources are listed so you can check them.
setup: Read access to your CRM and email. A list of sources you consider acceptable. Setup is often a day.
human_checks: The person meeting the prospect checks facts against the listed sources.
SI uses public and your own information only.
Anything uncertain is marked as such. It is not stated as fact.

examples.scenario: Before meeting a growing restaurant group, the brief notes the two new locations opening. It notes the current carrier mentioned in an old email. It lists questions about liquor liability.
A brief on a regional manufacturer covers its open job postings. It covers recent plant expansion news. It covers the last talk with its HR manager.
Before a school district interview, the brief summarizes the district's published facilities plan. It also covers past projects of similar size.

copy_prompt: Prepare a one-page brief on [organization] for a meeting on [date] with [names]. Use their website [URL], these public sources [list], and my CRM notes and emails about them. Include what they do, recent changes, who I am meeting, past contact with us, and [3] good questions. List sources for every fact. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Meetings start better prepared. There is less last-minute scrambling.

title: Personal outreach drafts and reply handling you approve
summary: SI drafts first-touch and follow-up messages from real research. It sorts the replies. It offers meeting times. You approve every message.
problem: Generic outreach gets ignored. Personal outreach takes too long to write. Replies, when they come, sit unsorted. Interested people go cold.
what_si_does: SI starts from a list of prospects and a short brief on each. It drafts a short first message that refers to something specific and relevant. It also drafts one or two follow-ups. When replies come in, it sorts them. Groups are interested, not now, wrong person, and no. It drafts an answer for each. For the interested ones, it proposes open times from your calendar. Unsubscribe and no-contact requests are recorded and respected.
setup: Your prospect list. Calendar access. A clear description of what you offer. Setup is often several days.
human_checks: Every message is approved before sending. Volume stays modest.
Opt-outs are honored immediately and recorded.
Outreach follows the anti-spam and privacy rules that apply to you.

examples.scenario: Drafts to office managers at nearby firms mention their recent move into a new building. They offer a tasting. Replies asking for menus get a draft with the menu and two tasting times.
Property managers of older buildings get a note about seasonal maintenance. A 'not now, try in spring' reply becomes a dated reminder.
Small nonprofits with an upcoming grant cycle get a short note. It offers a review of last year's application.

copy_prompt: For each prospect in [list] with these notes [research], draft a first message of under [100] words that mentions one specific, relevant detail and offers [offer]. Draft [2] short follow-ups. Then sort these replies [paste] into interested, not now, wrong person and no, and draft an answer for each, offering times from [calendar]. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Outreach becomes more personal without taking all afternoon. Interested replies get answered quickly.
caution: Outbound email and messaging are regulated. One example is CAN-SPAM in the US. Rules in the EU and Canada are stricter. Include opt-out handling. Follow the rules that apply to you.

title: Check-ins for repeat customers who are due
summary: SI spots regular customers who are past their usual reorder or rebooking interval. Then it drafts a friendly, specific check-in.
problem: Repeat customers are the easiest business to keep. Nobody tracks when each one is due. They drift away quietly. Or they simply buy from whoever reached out first.
what_si_does: SI reads your order, invoice, or appointment history. It works out each regular customer's usual interval. It lists those who are overdue. For each, it drafts a short check-in. The check-in mentions what they usually order or book. It offers an easy next step.
setup: An export of order, invoice, or booking history. Draft access to email or text. Setup is often a few days.
human_checks: A person reviews the list and approves each message.
Customers who asked not to be contacted are excluded.
Customers with open complaints or unpaid balances are flagged instead of nudged.

examples.scenario: A cafe that orders every two weeks has not ordered in four. The draft mentions their usual blend. It asks whether anything changed.
Customers who booked an opening last spring but not this spring get a reminder. Open dates are included.
Clients who usually book every six weeks and are now at nine get a text draft. It offers their stylist's next openings.

copy_prompt: Using this order or booking history [file], find each customer's usual interval between [orders/visits]. List customers who are more than [50%] past their usual interval, with their last date and usual purchase. Draft a short check-in for each in this tone: [example]. Exclude [do-not-contact list]. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Regular customers hear from you before they drift. The outreach feels personal rather than mass-mailed.

title: Supplier invoices from email into draft bills
summary: SI reads supplier invoices that arrive by email. It creates draft bills in your accounting tool. It flags duplicates or missing details.
problem: Invoices arrive as PDFs in several inboxes. Someone retypes them into the accounting system. Duplicates, typos, and missed due dates follow.
what_si_does: SI watches an invoices inbox. It reads each attachment. It extracts supplier, invoice number, date, due date, line totals, and tax. It creates a draft bill with a suggested account based on past coding. It checks for problems. Those include an invoice number already entered. They include an amount that does not match the purchase order. They include missing tax registration details. They include a changed bank account on the invoice.
setup: A dedicated invoices inbox or forwarding rule. Accounting access limited to creating drafts. Your past coding as a reference. Setup is often a few days.
human_checks: The bookkeeper reviews and approves each draft bill.
SI never pays bills. SI never changes supplier bank details.
A change in a supplier's payment details is always flagged. It is confirmed by phone with a known contact.

examples.scenario: Lumber and electrical supply invoices are turned into draft bills tagged to the right job. A second copy of the same invoice sent by a supplier's rep is caught.
Weekly produce, meat, and linen invoices become draft bills. Food and non-food costs are coded separately.
Vendor invoices for repairs are matched to the property and unit. One arriving with new bank details is flagged before anyone pays it.

copy_prompt: Read the invoices in [inbox/folder] from [date]. For each, extract supplier, invoice number, dates, totals and tax. Suggest an account using this past coding [file]. Flag duplicates (same supplier and number or amount), missing details, mismatches with [PO file], and any change in payment details. Prepare draft bills only. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Less retyping. Fewer duplicate payments. Payment-detail changes get a second look.

title: Matching receipts to card transactions
summary: SI matches receipts from email and photos to card transactions. It suggests categories. It lists what is still missing before month end.
problem: Card transactions pile up without receipts. At month end someone hunts through email and phone photos to match them. Expense reports are late.
what_si_does: SI reads receipts from a forwarding inbox or shared folder. It matches them to transactions by amount, date, and merchant. It suggests a category from past coding. It builds a missing-receipts list per cardholder. It can also assemble a simple expense report for staff who pay out of pocket.
setup: Card transaction feed or export. A receipts inbox or folder. The chart of accounts. Setup is often a few days.
human_checks: The bookkeeper confirms categories before anything is posted.
Reminders to cardholders about missing receipts are reviewed before sending.
Unusual or personal-looking charges are flagged for the owner.

examples.scenario: Fuel and hardware-store receipts snapped by field crews are matched to the company cards. Each crew lead gets a short list of what is missing.
Travel receipts from a client trip are matched. They are grouped into an expense report ready to be billed back to the client.
Program staff purchases are matched and coded to the right grant. Grant reports are easier at quarter end.

copy_prompt: Match these card transactions [export] to the receipts in [folder/inbox]. Match on amount, date (within [3] days) and merchant. Suggest a category using this past coding [file]. List unmatched transactions by cardholder, and flag anything unusual. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Month end has fewer surprises. Chasing receipts becomes a short list instead of a search.

title: Reminders for overdue invoices, firmer as they age
summary: SI checks open invoices each week. It drafts reminders whose tone matches how late each one is. You approve them.
problem: Chasing money is uncomfortable, so it gets put off. Invoices drift from 30 to 90 days late. By then the talk is harder.
what_si_does: SI reads open invoices and payment history. It groups them by how overdue they are. It drafts a reminder for each. A friendly note goes out just after the due date. A clearer one goes later. A firm one with next steps goes after that. It uses your terms. It skips customers with a payment plan or a dispute. It flags long-overdue accounts for a phone call.
setup: Read access to invoices in your accounting tool. Draft access to email. Your reminder schedule and terms. Setup is often a day or two.
human_checks: A person approves every reminder.
Disputed invoices, payment plans, and key accounts are excluded or handled personally.
SI never threatens action. Any collections step is the owner's decision.

examples.scenario: Three clients are a week past due. They get friendly reminders with the invoice attached. One 60 days late is flagged for the owner to call.
Patient balances after insurance get courteous statement reminders. Any account showing a pending insurance appeal is excluded.
Corporate clients get reminders addressed to their accounts-payable contact. The purchase order number is included.

copy_prompt: Here are open invoices [export] with customer, amount, due date and notes. Group them by days overdue: [1-14], [15-45], [46+]. Draft a reminder for each group in increasing firmness, using my terms [paste]. Exclude anything marked disputed or on a plan. List accounts over [60] days for a phone call. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Reminders go out on time without the owner having to write them. The hardest cases get personal attention.
caution: Medical and dental practices: patient billing messages must follow health-privacy rules. Debt collection is also regulated. Keep reminders factual. Leave collections decisions to the owner.

title: Finding work that was done but never invoiced
summary: SI compares completed jobs, time entries, or deliveries against invoices sent. It lists anything that was never billed.
problem: Small jobs, extra hours, and change orders get done. Then they are forgotten at billing time. Nobody notices the gap because nothing looks wrong.
what_si_does: SI lines up the record of work done against invoices issued. Work done can be closed job tickets, timesheets, delivery notes, or change orders. It lists items with no matching invoice. It lists partial billing. It lists hours logged above what was billed. It prepares draft invoices or a list for the billing person.
setup: Read access to the job, time, or delivery system. Read access to invoicing. Setup is often a few days. Most of that time is spent agreeing on how to match records.
human_checks: The owner or billing person confirms each item before any invoice is drafted or sent.
Work done as a courtesy or under warranty is marked so it is not flagged again.
Customer-facing invoices are approved before sending.

examples.scenario: A closed ticket for a water heater flush has no invoice. Two change orders on a bathroom job have no invoice. Drafts are prepared for the office manager.
Logged hours on a matter exceed what was billed last month. The gap is listed for the billing partner to review.
Rental extensions recorded at return were never added to the customer's invoice.

copy_prompt: Compare these completed jobs or time entries [export] with these invoices [export] for [period]. Match on [job number, client, date]. List work with no invoice, partial invoices, and hours logged above hours billed. Draft invoices only for items I confirm. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Less revenue slips away unnoticed. Billing reviews have something concrete to check.

title: Month-end close prep and the accountant's package
summary: SI prepares the month-end checklist. It notes reconciliation exceptions. It builds an indexed bundle of documents for the bookkeeper or accountant.
problem: Month end means chasing missing documents. It means explaining odd transactions. It means emailing files back and forth. It drags on. The accountant's questions arrive weeks later.
what_si_does: SI runs through your close checklist. It lists unreconciled bank lines with suggested matches. It lists uncategorized transactions with suggested categories. It lists missing receipts and bills. It lists balances that moved oddly from last month. It writes a short note on each exception. It gathers the month's statements, invoices, and receipts into one indexed folder for the accountant.
setup: Read access to the accounting tool, bank exports, and document folders. Your checklist. Setup is often about a week.
human_checks: The bookkeeper or accountant reviews every proposed match and category.
SI does not post journal entries.
The package is reviewed before it is shared.

examples.scenario: The package includes bank and card statements and supplier invoices. A note says lab fees are unusually high this month because of a batch of crowns.
Unreconciled lines include two customer deposits with suggested invoice matches. A raw-materials bill has no receiving record.
Payment-processor payouts are broken into sales, fees, and refunds. Then they reconcile against the bank deposits.

copy_prompt: For [month], go through my close checklist [paste]. List unreconciled bank lines with suggested matches, uncategorized transactions with suggested categories, missing receipts or bills, and balances that changed by more than [20%] from last month, with a short note on each. Gather statements and documents from [folders] into one indexed folder for the accountant. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Close tends to finish sooner. There are fewer rounds of questions from the accountant.

title: Tracking subscriptions, contracts and renewal dates
summary: SI finds repeating charges and contract renewal dates in statements and files. It warns you before anything renews on its own.
problem: Software subscriptions, service contracts, leases, and insurance policies often renew on their own. Nobody remembers what each one costs. Nobody knows if you still use it. Nobody knows when you must give notice.
what_si_does: SI scans card and bank statements for repeating charges. It reads contracts for term, renewal date, and notice dates. It builds one list with cost, owner, renewal date, and notice deadline. It flags duplicates and tools nobody seems to use. It sends a reminder well before each notice deadline.
setup: Statement exports and a folder of contracts. Setup is often a few days.
human_checks: A person decides what to cancel or renegotiate. SI never cancels anything.
A person checks contract dates SI pulls against the document.
Reminders go to the named owner of each contract.

examples.scenario: The list shows two overlapping document-sharing tools. It also flags a tax software license. That license renews just before busy season.
Elevator, landscaping, and insurance contracts across buildings sit on one list. Notice deadlines are there too. Renegotiation can start in time.
Seats for former staff on several design and project tools are flagged.

copy_prompt: Review these statements [files] for recurring charges, and these contracts [folder] for term, renewal and notice dates. Build one list with vendor, cost, frequency, owner, renewal date and notice deadline. Flag duplicates and anything with no clear owner. Set reminders [30] days before each notice deadline. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Fewer surprise renewals. Unused tools get noticed.
caution: Contract dates and terms SI pulls are a starting point. They are not a legal reading. Check the actual document. Ask a lawyer about anything unclear.

title: A year-end document packet for your tax preparer
summary: SI sorts the year's documents. It totals them by category. It flags gaps. Your tax preparer gets one organized packet.
problem: At tax time, documents sit in email, folders, and paper. The preparer sends a list of questions. Gathering the answers takes weeks.
what_si_does: SI goes through the year's folders and inbox for tax-related documents. It looks for income forms, statements, and receipts. It also looks for vehicle and home-office records. It looks for donation receipts and prior-year notices. It sorts and renames them. It builds an index and category totals. It lists what seems missing next to last year's packet. It does not decide what is deductible.
setup: Access to the relevant folders and inbox. Last year's packet or the preparer's checklist. Setup is often a few days.
human_checks: The owner and tax preparer review the packet. SI makes no tax judgments.
Sensitive documents are shared only through the preparer's secure channel.
Category totals are checked against source documents.

examples.scenario: Supply receipts, vehicle mileage logs, and 1099s from three general contractors are sorted. A note flags one 1099 from last year's client that has not arrived.
Payroll summaries, sales tax filings, and equipment purchase invoices are gathered. They match the accountant's checklist.
Repair invoices, insurance, and property tax bills are sorted by property.

copy_prompt: Using [folders/inbox], find tax-related documents for [year]. Sort and rename them by [category], build an index and category totals, and compare against this checklist [preparer's list or last year's packet] to list what is missing. Do not decide what is deductible. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Tax prep starts organized. The back-and-forth with the preparer tends to be shorter.
caution: Tax: SI organizes documents and drafts summaries. It does not give tax advice. It does not decide what is deductible. A qualified accountant or tax preparer makes those calls.

title: A one-page weekly snapshot for the owner
summary: Every Monday, SI pulls the numbers you care about from your tools. It puts them on one page. It adds short notes on what changed.
problem: The numbers that matter live in five different systems. Checking them takes a morning. So it does not happen regularly. Problems show up late.
what_si_does: SI collects a short, fixed set of measures each week. Examples are sales, new inquiries, and jobs completed. Also cash in the bank, overdue invoices, and open complaints. It lays them next to last week and the same week last year. It adds a few plain sentences on what moved and why, where the data shows it.
setup: Read access to the tools involved. An agreed list of no more than about ten measures. Setup is often about a week.
human_checks: The owner chooses the measures. The owner checks the first few reports against the source systems.
Notes are marked as likely causes, not certainties.
Access is read-only.

examples.scenario: The page shows car count, average repair order, and comebacks by location. A note says one shop's car count dropped. That was the week a technician was out.
Partners see returns in progress each Monday in tax season. They also see returns waiting on clients, billed hours, and unpaid invoices.
Sales by location and day. Food cost from supplier bills. Weather notes on slow days.

copy_prompt: Every [Monday], pull these measures [list] from [tools] for last week. Show each against the prior week and the same week last year. Write [3-5] plain sentences on what changed and the likely reasons visible in the data, marked as likely. Keep it to one page. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: The owner sees the business at a glance every week. Changes get noticed while they are still small.

title: One view of revenue across every place you take money
summary: SI puts sales from each channel, location, or payment system into one sheet or dashboard. The sheet updates on a set schedule.
problem: Money comes in through a point-of-sale system, online payments, and invoices. You may also have a marketplace or two. Each has its own report. None of them agree on the total.
what_si_does: SI pulls sales from each source. It maps them to shared categories. Categories can be location, product or service line, or channel. It removes counting twice. An invoice also logged as a card payment is one example. It keeps one table current. It keeps a simple dashboard current. It notes where sources do not match.
setup: Read access or regular exports from each source. An agreed set of categories. Setup is often one to two weeks.
human_checks: Totals are checked against the accounting system each month.
The owner reviews the category mapping.
Mismatches are reported, not quietly adjusted.

examples.scenario: Taproom sales, distributor invoices, and online merchandise sales appear together. They are shown by week and by product.
Lesson payments, recital ticket sales, and instrument rentals are combined. Family accounts paid by both card and check are not counted twice.
In-store sales, online orders, and a marketplace channel are combined by product category. Slow lines are easy to see across all three.

copy_prompt: Combine sales from these sources [exports or connections] for [period]. Map each to these categories [location, line, channel]. Remove double-counted payments by matching [invoice number, amount and date]. Build one table and a simple chart by [week]. List any discrepancies between sources. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: One trusted number for revenue. A clear picture of which channels or lines are growing.

title: Plain-language notes when a number moves
summary: When a key number jumps or drops, SI looks for likely reasons in the data. It writes a short, plain note for the owner.
problem: Dashboards show that something changed but not why. Someone has to dig through reports to find out. Often nobody does.
what_si_does: SI watches a few chosen numbers. When one moves past a threshold you set, it checks the obvious splits. Splits can be by location, product, customer, staff member, channel, or day. It writes a short note. The note says what changed. It says where the change is concentrated. It says what to look at next. It presents causes as possibilities.
setup: Read access to the source data. Thresholds for each number. Setup is often several days.
human_checks: Notes are labeled as possible explanations for a person to confirm.
Thresholds are adjusted to avoid noise.
No action is taken automatically.

examples.scenario: New-client visits dropped a lot this month. The note shows the drop is almost all from one referral source. That source stopped sending patients.
Food cost rose at one location. The note points to a price increase on one supplier's invoices. It also points to a menu item selling more than usual.
Monthly online donations fell. The note shows recurring donors whose cards expired.

copy_prompt: Watch these measures [list] in [data source]. When one changes by more than [threshold] versus [comparison period], break it down by [dimensions] and write a short note on where the change is concentrated and what to check next. Present causes as possibilities. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Changes get explained sooner. The owner spends less time digging through reports.

title: Ad spend next to real results, in one sheet
summary: SI lines up spend from each ad platform with the inquiries, bookings, or sales it produced. It lists campaigns that look weak.
problem: Each ad platform reports its own success. Those numbers are often generous. Comparing spend with real customers means joining exports by hand.
what_si_does: SI pulls spend by campaign from each platform. It matches it to results in your own systems. Results can be form leads, booked calls, or sales by source or promo code. It shows cost per lead or sale by campaign and week. It lists campaigns with spend but little real result. It adds suggestions to review.
setup: Read access or exports from the ad platforms and your lead or sales system. Consistent tracking such as source fields or codes. Setup is often about a week.
human_checks: A person makes budget changes. SI only recommends.
Attribution gaps are stated plainly.
Whoever runs the ads reviews the suggestions.

examples.scenario: Search ad spend by campaign is matched to signed intake forms rather than clicks. This shows which campaigns bring qualified calls.
Social ads in two towns produce plenty of leads but few booked cleanings. The sheet lists them for review.
Spend by campaign is compared with orders using the store's source tracking. The platforms' own numbers sit next to them.

copy_prompt: Combine ad spend by campaign and week from [platforms/exports] with results from [lead or sales system] matched by [source, campaign tag or code]. Show cost per [lead/booking/sale] by campaign. List campaigns with spend above [amount] and few results, with suggestions. Note any gaps in tracking. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Ad decisions rest on real customers. Weak campaigns are easier to spot.
caution: Law firms and health practices: advertising is subject to professional and privacy rules. Tracking tools must not send protected client or patient information to ad platforms.

title: A weekly watch on competitors' prices and offers
summary: Once a week SI checks the competitor pages you choose. It sends a short summary of changed prices, services, offers, or openings.
problem: Owners know competitors matter. They rarely have time to check their sites. Price changes and new offers are noticed months later. Usually a customer is the one who mentions it.
what_si_does: SI visits a fixed list of public competitor pages. Pages can cover pricing, menus, service lists, promotions, and job postings. It compares them with last week's snapshot. It records changes in a sheet. It sends a short summary of what is new, with links.
setup: A list of competitors and pages to watch. Setup is often a day or two.
human_checks: SI only reads public pages. It respects site terms.
Pricing decisions remain with the owner.
The watch list is reviewed every few months.

examples.scenario: Two nearby practices started advertising new-patient whitening offers. One now lists evening hours.
A competitor's posted rates for local moves went up. Another added a storage service.
Event calendars of nearby shops and libraries are tracked. Author events do not clash.

copy_prompt: Every [week], check these public pages [list of URLs] and compare them with last week's version. Record changes in prices, services, offers, hours and job postings in [sheet]. Send me a short summary with links. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Competitor changes are noticed in weeks rather than months.

title: A weekly team report from the tools you already use
summary: SI pulls updates from project, support, and sales tools. It drafts a weekly report. A manager edits it and sends it.
problem: Writing the weekly update means asking everyone for status. It also means copying from several tools. It takes a manager's afternoon. The result is often late or thin.
what_si_does: SI reads what changed during the week. It reads tasks completed and overdue in the project tool. It reads tickets opened and closed. It reads deals moved. It reads notes from team channels. It drafts a report with highlights, risks, overdue items, and decisions needed. It uses the format your team already uses.
setup: Read access to the tools involved. An example of a good past report. Setup is often several days.
human_checks: The manager edits and sends the report.
A person words risks and personnel matters.
SI does not post to shared channels without approval.

examples.scenario: The Friday report lists each job's progress. It lists inspections passed or pending. It lists change orders. It lists material delays from supplier emails.
Client projects are summarized. The summary covers deliverables shipped, items waiting on clients, and hours used against budget.
Volunteer hours, events held, and grant deliverables due next month go into the director's update.

copy_prompt: Read this week's activity in [project tool, helpdesk, CRM, channels]. Draft a weekly report in this format [example] with highlights, risks, overdue items and decisions needed. Keep it under [one page]. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Reports go out on time with less effort. Overdue items are visible to everyone.

title: Monthly themes from customer questions, complaints and surveys
summary: SI groups a month of support messages, reviews, and survey answers by theme. It counts them. It suggests what to fix at the source.
problem: The same problems create complaints month after month. Nobody steps back to count them. Fixes target whatever was loudest, not what was most common.
what_si_does: SI reads the month's tickets, emails, reviews, and survey comments. It groups them by root cause. Causes can be billing confusion, late arrivals, unclear instructions, or a product defect. It counts each group. It quotes a few representative examples. It suggests one or two upstream fixes for the biggest themes.
setup: Exports from the helpdesk, review sites, or survey tool. Setup is often a few days.
human_checks: The owner decides which themes to act on.
Personal details are removed from quoted examples.
Theme groupings are checked against a sample of raw messages.

examples.scenario: Many calls this month were about how to read the new online lab results. That suggests a short guide for parents.
Complaints group into missed arrival windows and surprise charges for stairs. That points to clearer quotes.
End-of-course evaluations show repeated requests for evening sections. They also ask for earlier access to materials.

copy_prompt: Here are this month's support messages, reviews and survey comments [exports]. Group them by underlying cause, count each group, and quote [2] representative examples with personal details removed. Suggest [1-2] upstream fixes for the largest groups. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Recurring problems become visible and easy to count. That makes it easier to fix them at the source.

title: Drafting next week's staff schedule from availability
summary: SI collects when people can work and time-off requests. It drafts next week's schedule against your coverage rules. A manager adjusts it.
problem: Building the schedule means matching texts, time-off requests, and coverage needs. It also means matching when people can work. It eats a manager's evening. It still leaves gaps.
what_si_does: SI gathers when people can work and requests from a form or shared sheet. It applies your rules. Rules can include minimum coverage per shift. They can include required skills or certifications, maximum hours, and fair rotation of weekends. It drafts a schedule. It lists any shift it could not fill. It lists any rule it had to bend. The manager decides.
setup: A form or sheet for when people can work. Your coverage rules. The scheduling tool or sheet. Setup is often several days.
human_checks: The manager reviews and publishes the schedule.
A person decides overtime and rule exceptions.
The manager confirms labor rules such as required breaks and minors' hours.

examples.scenario: Servers' availability and two time-off requests produce a draft. A trained bartender is on every shift. A Saturday double is flagged as overtime.
Caregiver availability is matched against client visit times and travel areas. One uncovered visit is flagged.
Weekend shifts rotate fairly across part-timers. Holiday coverage is drafted a month ahead.

copy_prompt: Using this availability [sheet/form responses] and these time-off requests [list], draft a schedule for [week] that meets these rules [coverage, skills, max hours, rotation]. List unfilled shifts and any rule you could not meet. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Schedules come together faster. Gaps are visible before the week starts.

title: Turning how-we-do-it into written procedures
summary: SI turns a recorded walkthrough, voice memo, or screen recording into a clear, step-by-step procedure. Your team can follow it.
problem: Know-how lives in a few people's heads. Training is slow. Mistakes repeat. The business depends on whoever remembers how things are done.
what_si_does: A team member records themselves doing the task, or just talks it through. SI turns the recording or transcript into a numbered procedure. It includes purpose, tools needed, steps, checks, common mistakes, and who to ask. It lists steps that seemed unclear so the expert can fill them in.
setup: A way to record, such as a phone, screen recorder, or video call. A shared place for procedures. Setup is often a day.
human_checks: The expert reviews each procedure before it is shared.
Safety-related steps are checked by whoever is responsible for safety.
Procedures are dated. They are reviewed when processes change.

examples.scenario: The head baker narrates the opening routine. SI writes a procedure covering oven checks, proofing times, and allergen cleaning.
A screen recording of submitting a claim correction becomes a step-by-step guide. Screenshots are referenced.
The move-out inspection process becomes a checklist. It includes photo requirements per room.

copy_prompt: Here is a transcript or recording of [person] doing [task]: [file]. Write a procedure with purpose, tools needed, numbered steps, checks, common mistakes and who to ask. List any steps that are unclear. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Training gets easier. The business depends less on one person remembering everything.

title: Appointment confirmations, reminders and reschedules
summary: SI sends approved confirmation and reminder messages. It handles reschedule requests against your real calendar. It keeps the schedule current.
problem: No-shows and last-minute changes waste slots. Staff spend time calling to confirm. They also juggle reschedules over text, email, and phone.
what_si_does: SI sends confirmations and reminders from approved templates. It sends them at set times before each appointment. It reads replies. It handles simple reschedules by offering open slots that fit your rules. Rules can include provider, room, and length. Anything unusual goes to staff. That includes a request to change the type of appointment or a complaint.
setup: Calendar or booking-system access. Approved templates. Reschedule rules. Setup is often a few days to a week.
human_checks: A person approves templates once. Anything outside them goes to staff.
Staff handle cancellations within the fee window.
Messages contain only what the client needs to know.

examples.scenario: Patients get a reminder two days before. A patient who replies that she has a conflict is offered three openings with the same hygienist.
Drop-off confirmations go out the day before. They include a note about the shuttle schedule.
Families get reminders. A reschedule request is matched to the same tutor's open slots.

copy_prompt: Using [calendar/booking system], draft confirmation and reminder messages for appointments [timing, e.g. 48 hours before]. For reschedule replies, offer [3] open slots that match [provider, length, location]. Send anything else to [staff]. Show me the templates and the first day's messages. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Fewer no-shows and less phone tag. Staff handle only the unusual changes.
caution: Medical and dental offices: reminder messages should follow health-privacy rules. HIPAA in the US is one example. Keep details minimal. Use approved channels.

title: Meeting notes into owners and due dates
summary: SI turns a meeting transcript or rough notes into a short summary. It lists decisions and a task list with owners and due dates.
problem: Meetings end with agreement. Then nothing happens because nobody wrote down who would do what. The next meeting starts by talking through the last one again.
what_si_does: From a transcript or notes, SI writes a short summary. It lists decisions made, open questions, and action items. Each action item has an owner and due date. It can post the summary to the team channel once approved. It can add tasks to the project tool once approved. It starts the next agenda with any items still open.
setup: Access to transcripts or notes, the team channel, and the task tool. Setup is often a day.
human_checks: The meeting organizer reviews the summary before it is shared.
Task owners confirm their tasks.
Recording is used only with participants' consent.

examples.scenario: Board meeting notes become draft minutes. They also become a list of motions and votes, and action items for committee chairs.
The weekly site meeting with subcontractors produces a list. It shows who is fixing which punch-list item by when.
The partner meeting's decisions about client assignments are logged. Tasks are created.

copy_prompt: Here is the transcript or notes from [meeting]: [paste]. Write a short summary, decisions, open questions and action items with owner and due date. Draft a post for [channel] and the tasks for [tool]. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Decisions stick. Follow-through is easier to track.
caution: Recording meetings: consent rules vary by place. Tell participants. Follow the stricter rule if unsure. Formal board minutes should be reviewed by the secretary.

title: Turning meeting requests and forwarded emails into calendar holds
summary: When an email asks to meet or includes a date, SI drafts the reply with real open times. It creates a tentative calendar hold for you to confirm.
problem: Scheduling takes several back-and-forth emails. Dates buried in emails, flyers, and attachments never make it onto the calendar.
what_si_does: SI reads incoming messages and forwarded items for meeting requests, deadlines, and event dates. For meeting requests it checks your calendar. It drafts a reply with a few times that fit your rules. For dates in forwarded emails or attachments, it creates tentative events. Each has the details and a link back to the source.
setup: Calendar and email access with draft permissions. Your scheduling preferences. Setup is often a day.
human_checks: Holds stay tentative until you confirm.
Replies are approved before sending.
SI does not accept invitations on your behalf.

examples.scenario: A buyer's email asking to see two houses on Saturday becomes a draft reply. The reply has three time windows and tentative holds.
A forwarded court notice becomes a calendar entry. It has the hearing date and a reminder a week before.
Dates from a forwarded school newsletter become tentative events on the association's calendar.

copy_prompt: Read [inbox/forwarded messages]. For each meeting request, draft a reply offering [3] times that fit [rules] in my calendar. For each date or deadline mentioned, create a tentative event with the details and a link to the source. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Less back-and-forth to set meetings. Fewer dates fall off the calendar.
caution: Legal deadlines: SI-created entries are a convenience. They are not a docketing system. An attorney must confirm court and filing deadlines.

title: A morning briefing across inbox, calendar and tasks
summary: Each morning SI prepares a short briefing. It covers today's meetings, urgent messages, overdue tasks, and stalled deals.
problem: Owners start the day reacting to whatever is on top of the inbox. Prep for meetings happens in the car. Overdue items surface late.
what_si_does: SI reads today's calendar, recent email, the task list, and the CRM. It writes a short briefing. It lists meetings with context on each attendee. It lists messages that need a reply today. It lists tasks overdue or due today. It lists deals or projects with no activity for a while. It is sent at a set time by email or chat.
setup: Read access to calendar, email, tasks, and CRM. Setup is often a day or two.
human_checks: The briefing is read-only. Any follow-up action is approved.
Confidential threads can be excluded.
Content is reviewed after the first week. It is trimmed to what is useful.

examples.scenario: The briefing lists two commercial bids due this week. It lists a call with a supplier rep. It lists three customer complaints from yesterday.
Today's donor meeting comes with the donor's giving history and last conversation notes.
Client meetings come with notes from the last review. The list shows clients who emailed with questions.

copy_prompt: Every morning at [time], read my calendar, email from the last [24 hours], tasks and [CRM]. Write a short briefing: today's meetings with context, messages needing a reply today, overdue tasks, and deals or projects with no activity in [14] days. Send it to [email/chat]. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: The day starts with a plan. Meetings start better prepared.

title: Turning incoming work and maintenance requests into scheduled jobs
summary: SI turns work requests from email, forms, and messages into job tickets. It sorts them by urgency. It drafts a schedule and customer updates.
problem: Requests arrive by phone, text, email, and portal. They get written on paper, entered late, or lost. Customers do not know when someone is coming.
what_si_does: SI reads each request. It creates a job ticket with the location, problem, urgency, and any photos. It checks capacity or vendor availability. It proposes a time slot or the right vendor by your rules. It drafts the message to the customer or tenant with the plan. It drafts the dispatch note to the technician or vendor.
setup: Access to the request channels. The job or maintenance system. Your urgency and assignment rules. Setup is often one to two weeks.
human_checks: A dispatcher or manager approves assignments and customer messages.
Emergencies follow your escalation rules. A person confirms them.
Vendor work orders above a set amount need approval.

examples.scenario: A tenant's email about a leaking kitchen faucet becomes a ticket marked routine. It is assigned to the plumbing vendor. A draft reply gives the expected visit window.
A client's request for an extra floor-waxing visit is scheduled into the next open night crew slot.
Teacher requests for repairs are logged by building and room. They are grouped into the custodian's weekly plan.

copy_prompt: For each request in [channels], create a ticket with location, problem, urgency per [rules], and attachments. Propose a time or vendor using [capacity calendar or vendor list]. Draft a message to the requester with the plan, and a dispatch note to the assignee. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Requests are captured and acknowledged in a consistent way. Customers know what to expect.

title: Reorder lists from sales pace
summary: On a set schedule, SI turns recent usage or sales and stock on hand into a suggested reorder list. The list is grouped by supplier. You approve it.
problem: Reordering happens from memory or a quick look at the shelf. Fast movers run out. Slow movers get reordered anyway. Nobody has time to do the math across hundreds of items.
what_si_does: SI reads recent sales or usage per item. It reads stock on hand and on order. It reads each supplier's lead time and minimum order. It works out how many days of stock remain. It flags anything that will run out before the next delivery could arrive. It drafts a reorder list per supplier. Each line has a short reason. One example: using faster than last month, about nine days left, three-week lead time.
setup: Read access to sales or usage data. That can be point of sale, order system, job records, or a stock sheet. Plus one sheet of suppliers, lead times, pack sizes, and minimums. Agree on how much stock to keep per item group. Setup is often about a week including tuning.
human_checks: The buyer or owner reviews every line. They edit quantities before anything goes to a supplier.
SI only drafts. It does not place orders.
Seasonal and discontinued items are marked so they are not suggested blindly.

examples.scenario: Weekly usage from the point-of-sale system and the last inventory count produce a list. The list covers produce, dry goods, and paper suppliers. A note says the brunch menu is using eggs faster.
Gloves, impression material, and sterilization pouches are tracked from monthly counts. The order is drafted before the distributor's cutoff.
Units sold per variant over the last 30 and 90 days and current stock produce a reorder list per supplier. Three variants that will run out before restock are flagged.

copy_prompt: Using this sales or usage data [file] for the last [90] days and my stock on hand [file], estimate days of stock left for each item. Use these lead times and minimums [supplier sheet]. Draft a reorder list grouped by supplier with a one-line reason for each item, and flag anything with less than [14] days left. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Reordering becomes a short review instead of a long spreadsheet session. Shortages on fast movers tend to be caught earlier. Results depend on how clean the lead-time data is.

title: Drafting purchase orders without a dedicated purchasing system
summary: SI turns an approved reorder list into supplier-ready purchase orders in your format. It tracks what is open. It drafts the emails.
problem: Many businesses order by phone, text, or a quick email with no purchase order. Nobody can say what is on order. Nobody can say what price was agreed or what arrived. That is worse when a purchasing tool is retired or was never set up.
what_si_does: From an approved list, SI builds a purchase order per supplier. Each has item codes, quantities, agreed prices, and delivery address. They are numbered and saved to a shared folder. It drafts the email to each supplier. It keeps an open-orders sheet. It updates the sheet when confirmations or shipping notices arrive.
setup: A purchase order template. A supplier list with contacts and item codes. A shared folder or sheet. Setup is often a few days.
human_checks: A person approves each purchase order before it is sent.
Price changes on supplier confirmations are flagged.
SI never accepts new terms. It never changes quantities on its own.

examples.scenario: Materials for two upcoming jobs are combined into one purchase order per supply house. Each line is tagged to the job.
Orders to five small producers go out as consistent purchase orders. The open-orders sheet shows which ones have confirmed.
Paper and ink orders are drafted from the reorder list with the distributor's item codes.

copy_prompt: From this approved reorder list [file], create one purchase order per supplier using [template], with PO number, item codes, quantities, agreed prices from [price sheet] and delivery address [address]. Draft the email to each supplier and add each PO to [open-orders sheet]. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Ordering becomes traceable. Everyone can see what is on order, at what price, and when it is due.

title: Checking deliveries against what was ordered
summary: When a delivery arrives, SI compares the packing slip or invoice with the purchase order. It lists shortages, substitutions, and price differences.
problem: Deliveries get signed for without a careful count. Shortages, wrong items, and price increases are found weeks later. That is after the invoice is paid.
what_si_does: Staff snap a photo of the packing slip or forward the supplier invoice. SI reads it. It matches it line by line to the purchase order. It lists anything short, extra, substituted, backordered, or priced differently. It drafts a note to the supplier for credits or missing items. It updates the open-orders sheet.
setup: Open purchase orders in a sheet or system. A phone or email path for packing slips. Setup is often a few days.
human_checks: Staff confirm physical counts. SI only compares paperwork.
Credit requests are approved before sending.
Invoices with differences are held for review before payment.

examples.scenario: The fish delivery is two kilos short. The produce invoice shows a higher price on lemons. Both are flagged before the invoice is entered.
A pallet arrives with a substituted brand of fasteners. The note to the distributor asks for confirmation of price.
A supply order arrives with one item backordered. The clinic manager is alerted so the item can be sourced elsewhere.

copy_prompt: Compare this packing slip or invoice [photo/PDF] with purchase order [number or file]. List lines that are short, extra, substituted, backordered or priced differently. Draft a note to [supplier] asking for credit or the missing items. Update [open-orders sheet]. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Supplier mistakes are caught while they can still be fixed. Invoices are paid for what actually arrived.

title: A daily watch for low stock and stuck orders
summary: Each day SI checks for items running low. It also checks orders or jobs that have stalled. It sends a short list with suggested fixes before customers notice.
problem: Problems are found when a customer complains. An item sold that was not in stock. A shipment stuck for a week. A job waiting on a part nobody ordered.
what_si_does: SI checks stock levels against minimums. It compares open customer orders or jobs with the stock and parts they need. It looks for orders with no movement beyond a set time. No shipping scan or no status change counts as no movement. It sends a short daily list. The list says what is wrong and a suggested next step. Examples are contacting the customer, transferring stock, or chasing a carrier.
setup: Read access to stock and order or job data. Carrier tracking if relevant. Setup is often several days.
human_checks: A person decides on each fix. They approve any customer message.
Staff make stock changes in the system.
Thresholds are tuned to avoid false alarms.

examples.scenario: Two customer orders depend on a part with zero stock and no open purchase order. The list suggests ordering and warning the customers.
A delivery has shown no carrier update for six days. A draft message to the customer and a carrier inquiry are prepared.
Three scheduled repairs need a part not yet received. The dispatcher can reschedule before the technician drives out.
